title: Docker
description: Master Docker from container fundamentals through Dockerfiles, BuildKit, storage, networking, Compose, secure development workflows, production operations, and systematic troubleshooting.

paths.title: Docker Foundations
paths.description: Understand images, containers, the Docker client/daemon model, isolation, lifecycle, and the core CLI.

paths.title: Images, Dockerfiles & Builds
paths.description: Build reproducible images with Dockerfiles, small build contexts, cache-aware layers, multi-stage builds, tags, digests, and multi-platform tooling.

paths.title: Container Runtime & Lifecycle
paths.description: Run and operate containers with ports, environment, logs, exec, signals, restart behavior, resource limits, and health checks.

paths.title: Storage & Persistent Data
paths.description: Choose correctly among writable layers, named volumes, bind mounts, tmpfs, backups, and filesystem permissions.

paths.title: Docker Networking
paths.description: Understand bridge networks, service discovery, published ports, DNS, localhost boundaries, and network troubleshooting.

paths.title: Docker Compose
paths.description: Define and operate multi-container applications with services, networks, volumes, health dependencies, configuration, and lifecycle commands.

paths.title: Development Workflows
paths.description: Use Docker effectively for local development, live reload, dependency isolation, test environments, and reproducible onboarding.

paths.title: Security & Supply Chain
paths.description: Reduce privilege and attack surface, protect secrets, scan dependencies, pin artifacts, and understand rootless Docker and image provenance.

paths.title: Production Operations
paths.description: Promote immutable images, handle graceful shutdown, observability, backups, rollouts, resource controls, and registry workflows.

paths.title: Troubleshooting & Maintenance
paths.description: Diagnose container, build, network, storage, and platform problems using inspection tools and safe cleanup practices.

paths.title: Project: Containerize a Node API
paths.description: Apply the foundations to containerize and run a Node.js API with an efficient development-to-production image workflow.

paths.title: Project: API + PostgreSQL with Compose
paths.description: Build a realistic two-service stack with service discovery, health checks, persistent database storage, and environment configuration.

cards.title: Install Docker and verify the engine
cards.prompt: What should you verify after installing Docker Desktop or Docker Engine?
cards.content: Installation differs by operating system. Use Docker's supported installation path for your platform, then verify both client and server connectivity before troubleshooting application images.
steps: Install Docker Desktop or Docker Engine using the official instructions for your OS.
Open Docker Desktop or start the Docker Engine service if required.
Run `docker version` and confirm both Client and Server sections are available.
Run `docker info` to inspect the active engine and storage/runtime configuration.
Run a small test container such as `docker run --rm hello-world`.

cards.title: Docker packages processes with their runtime environment
cards.prompt: What problem does Docker solve?
cards.content: Docker lets you package an application, its filesystem, runtime, libraries, and startup configuration into an image, then run that image as an isolated container. This reduces environment drift between developers, CI, and deployment targets.

cards.title: An image is a template; a container is a running instance
cards.prompt: Distinguish a Docker image from a Docker container.
cards.content: An image is an immutable, content-addressed filesystem plus metadata. A container adds runtime configuration and a writable layer to an image. You can create many containers from the same image.

cards.title: Containers share a kernel rather than emulating an entire machine
cards.prompt: Why are containers usually lighter than full virtual machines?
cards.content: Linux containers isolate processes with kernel features such as namespaces and cgroups. They do not normally boot a separate guest kernel for every container. Docker Desktop still uses a Linux VM where the host OS is not Linux.

cards.title: Docker uses a client and an engine
cards.prompt: What happens when you run a docker CLI command?
cards.content: The Docker CLI sends API requests to a Docker Engine daemon or another configured Docker endpoint. The engine manages images, containers, networks, and volumes. The client may be on a different machine from the daemon.

cards.title: OCI standards make container artifacts and runtimes interoperable
cards.prompt: Where does Docker fit relative to OCI?
cards.content: The Open Container Initiative defines specifications for image formats, runtime behavior, and distribution. Docker uses OCI-compatible building blocks, which helps images and runtimes interoperate across container tooling.

cards.title: Namespaces isolate views; cgroups account and limit resources
cards.prompt: Which Linux primitives underpin much container isolation?
cards.content: Namespaces isolate views of process IDs, networking, mounts, hostnames, users, and other resources. Cgroups organize processes for resource accounting and limits such as CPU and memory. Containers combine these controls with filesystem and security mechanisms.

cards.title: Run a disposable container
cards.prompt: Use the CLI to run a short-lived command in an Alpine container.
cards.content: The --rm flag removes the stopped container automatically. The command after the image name replaces the image's default command for this run.

code.snippet: docker run --rm alpine:3.22 echo "hello from a container"

cards.title: Pull an image before running it
cards.prompt: How do you fetch and inspect a registry image explicitly?
cards.content: docker run pulls a missing image automatically, but an explicit pull makes artifact acquisition visible and can be useful in deployment or troubleshooting workflows.

code.snippet:
docker pull nginx:alpine
docker image inspect nginx:alpine

cards.title: Container names provide stable local references
cards.prompt: Why use `--name` instead of relying only on generated IDs?
cards.content: Human-readable names make logs, exec, stop, inspect, and network references easier. Names must be unique within an engine until the old container is removed or renamed.

cards.title: Learn the basic container lifecycle
cards.prompt: What is the normal create-start-stop-remove lifecycle?
cards.content: A container has identity and metadata even when it is stopped. Removing the container deletes that container object, not the underlying image.
steps: Create and start with `docker run`.
List running containers with `docker ps`.
List all containers with `docker ps -a`.
Stop gracefully with `docker stop <name>`.
Start an existing stopped container with `docker start <name>`.
Remove it with `docker rm <name>` when no longer needed.

cards.title: Image or container?
cards.prompt: Which statement is correct?

options: An image changes every time its container writes a file.
A container is a runtime instance created from an image.
A container registry runs your containers for you.
Every container includes its own guest kernel.
question.explanation: A container is created from an image and adds runtime state plus a writable layer.

cards.title: Registries distribute images
cards.prompt: What role does a container registry play?
cards.content: A registry stores and serves container image manifests and layers. Docker Hub is the default public registry for unqualified image names, but organizations also use private or cloud registries.

cards.title: Inspect local Docker state
cards.prompt: Which commands show the most useful basic inventory?
cards.content: Use specific list and inspect commands before deleting or troubleshooting resources.

code.snippet:
docker ps
docker ps -a
docker image ls
docker volume ls
docker network ls
docker system df

cards.title: Docker contexts select which engine the CLI controls
cards.prompt: Why does `docker ps` sometimes show a different machine's containers?
cards.content: The CLI can target local or remote Docker endpoints through contexts. Always confirm the active context before making destructive changes, especially when production engines are reachable.

cards.title: Inspect and switch Docker contexts
cards.prompt: How do you see the active Docker endpoint?
cards.content: A context bundles endpoint and related CLI configuration. The asterisk in `docker context ls` marks the active context.

code.snippet:
docker context ls
docker context show
docker context use default

cards.title: Foundation mental model
cards.prompt: Verify the core distinctions before moving on.
cards.content: Most Docker confusion disappears when image, container, registry, engine, and host boundaries are kept separate.
items: Image = immutable packaged artifact.
Container = runtime instance of an image.
Registry = image distribution service.
Docker Engine = resource manager and runtime API.
Docker CLI = client of the engine.
Host = machine or VM where the engine runs.

cards.title: Dockerfiles describe image construction
cards.prompt: What is a Dockerfile?
cards.content: A Dockerfile is an ordered set of build instructions. Common instructions include FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, ENV, USER, EXPOSE, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, and HEALTHCHECK.

cards.title: Image layers are content-addressed and shared
cards.prompt: Why can multiple images reuse disk efficiently?
cards.content: Immutable image layers are identified by content and can be shared when images reference the same layer data. A container adds its own writable layer without copying the entire image filesystem.

cards.title: A production-minded Node.js Dockerfile
cards.prompt: How can a Node application use separate dependency and runtime stages?
cards.content: Multi-stage builds let the final image contain only the runtime files needed to execute the app. Pin a real Node version appropriate to the project instead of relying on an unbounded latest tag.

code.snippet:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

FROM node:22-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

cards.title: Each Dockerfile instruction can contribute a cacheable layer
cards.prompt: Why does Dockerfile instruction order matter?
cards.content: When an early layer changes, later dependent layers usually need rebuilding. Copy stable dependency manifests and install dependencies before copying frequently changing application source so expensive layers can stay cached.

cards.title: .dockerignore keeps build context small
cards.prompt: What should usually be excluded from a Node build context?
cards.content: The build context is data sent to the builder. Exclude local dependencies, VCS metadata, secrets, logs, and other files that the image does not need.

code.snippet:
node_modules
.git
.env
*.log
coverage
Dockerfile*
compose*.yaml

cards.title: COPY is usually preferred for ordinary file copies
cards.prompt: When should ADD be avoided?
cards.content: Use COPY when you only need to copy files from the build context or another stage. ADD has additional behaviors such as remote URL handling and archive extraction, so use it only when those semantics are intentional.

cards.title: Multi-stage builds separate build tools from runtime
cards.prompt: Why use more than one FROM instruction?
cards.content: Each FROM begins a new build stage. You can compile, test, or generate assets in one stage and copy only the resulting artifacts into a lean runtime stage, reducing final image size and attack surface.

cards.title: Build cache ordering
cards.prompt: Which Dockerfile order usually gives better dependency-cache reuse for Node.js?

options: COPY . . then RUN npm ci
COPY package*.json ./ then RUN npm ci then COPY . .
RUN npm ci before copying package files
Disable the build cache for every build
question.explanation: Dependency installation can remain cached until the package manifests change.

cards.title: Tags are names; digests identify exact image content
cards.prompt: How do tags differ from image digests?
cards.content: A tag such as app:1.4 is a mutable reference that can be moved to another image. A digest such as sha256:... is content-addressed and identifies an exact manifest. Use digests when exact artifact identity matters.

cards.title: Build and tag an image
cards.prompt: Build an application image using the current directory as context.
cards.content: The final dot is the build context. The -t option creates a human-readable repository and tag reference.

code.snippet:
docker build -t my-api:1.0 .
docker image inspect my-api:1.0

cards.title: EXPOSE documents intended ports but does not publish them
cards.prompt: Does EXPOSE make a service reachable from the host?
cards.content: No. EXPOSE is image metadata describing intended listening ports. Use docker run -p/--publish or Compose ports to create host port mappings.

cards.title: BuildKit improves modern Docker builds
cards.prompt: What does the modern builder add?
cards.content: BuildKit supports efficient parallel execution, advanced caching, build secrets, SSH mounts, cache mounts, named contexts, and better multi-platform workflows. Modern Docker installations use BuildKit-backed build tooling.

cards.title: Build for multiple CPU architectures
cards.prompt: How can buildx create a multi-platform image?
cards.content: A multi-platform image tag points to a manifest index containing platform-specific images. The builder needs appropriate drivers/emulation or native workers.

code.snippet:
docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t registry.example.com/team/my-api:1.0 \
  --push .

cards.title: Build secrets are temporary build inputs
cards.prompt: How should a private package token be supplied during a BuildKit build?
cards.content: Use a secret mount for the specific RUN step that needs the credential. Do not pass sensitive credentials through ARG or ENV when they would become part of image configuration or build history.

code.snippet:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc \
    npm ci

cards.title: Publish a container port to the host
cards.prompt: Run nginx and map host port 8080 to container port 80.
cards.content: Published ports are explicit host-to-container mappings. Binding to 127.0.0.1 limits access to the local host; binding broadly may expose the service on host interfaces.

code.snippet: docker run -d --name web -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx:alpine

cards.title: Container localhost means the container itself
cards.prompt: Why does localhost often break container-to-container connections?
cards.content: Inside a container, 127.0.0.1/localhost refers to that same container's network namespace. To reach another container, use its network-resolvable name on a shared Docker network.

cards.title: Pass environment configuration at runtime
cards.prompt: How can a container receive a non-secret environment value?
cards.content: Environment variables are convenient configuration, but they can be visible through process/container metadata. Do not treat plain environment variables or checked-in env files as a complete secret-management strategy.

code.snippet:
docker run --rm \
  -e APP_ENV=development \
  -e PORT=3000 \
  my-api:1.0

cards.title: Read container logs
cards.prompt: How do you follow logs from a running container?
cards.content: Applications should normally write operational logs to stdout and stderr so the container runtime can collect and route them.

code.snippet: docker logs --tail 100 -f my-api

cards.title: Execute a diagnostic process inside a running container
cards.prompt: How do you open a shell for troubleshooting?
cards.content: docker exec starts an additional process in an existing container. Minimal images may not include bash; use sh if available.

code.snippet: docker exec -it my-api sh

cards.title: PID 1 must handle signals correctly
cards.prompt: Why can container shutdown behavior be surprising?
cards.content: The container's main process is PID 1 in its namespace. It should receive and handle termination signals, reap child processes when needed, and exit within the orchestrator's grace period. Exec-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT helps avoid unnecessary shell signal-handling problems.

cards.title: CMD vs docker run command override
cards.prompt: What happens when a command is supplied after the image name in docker run?

options: It always creates a new image.
It usually replaces CMD arguments for that container run.
It publishes every EXPOSE port.
It changes the Dockerfile on disk.
question.explanation: Runtime command arguments can override an image's default CMD, subject to ENTRYPOINT behavior.

cards.title: Restart policies control daemon-managed restarts
cards.prompt: What does a restart policy do?
cards.content: Policies such as no, on-failure, always, and unless-stopped tell Docker when to restart a stopped container. They are not a substitute for readiness checks, durable state, or an orchestrator's deployment logic.

cards.title: Apply CPU and memory limits
cards.prompt: How can you prevent one container from consuming all host resources?
cards.content: Resource flags use kernel controls to constrain a container. Tune limits from observed workload behavior rather than guessing; too-low memory limits can trigger OOM termination.

code.snippet:
docker run --rm \
  --memory=512m \
  --cpus=1.5 \
  my-api:1.0

cards.title: Health checks report container health separately from process existence
cards.prompt: Why add a HEALTHCHECK?
cards.content: A running process can still be unable to serve useful work. A health check periodically runs a command and records healthy/unhealthy state. Keep checks meaningful, fast, and independent of unnecessary external dependencies.

cards.title: Inspect a container's effective configuration
cards.prompt: Which command reveals mounts, networks, environment, state, and runtime metadata?
cards.content: docker inspect returns structured JSON. Use --format for focused fields when automating diagnostics.

code.snippet:
docker inspect my-api
docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' my-api

cards.title: Runtime hygiene
cards.prompt: What should a well-behaved application container do?
cards.content: Containers are easiest to replace and operate when they have a clear main process, explicit configuration, bounded resources, externalized persistent state, and predictable shutdown.
items: Run one primary service responsibility per container.
Keep persistent data outside the writable container layer.
Write logs to stdout/stderr.
Handle SIGTERM and graceful shutdown.
Use explicit port mappings.
Set appropriate resource limits.
Define health checks where they add meaningful signal.

cards.title: The container writable layer is ephemeral
cards.prompt: Where do files go when a container writes without a mount?
cards.content: Writes land in the container's writable layer above the image's read-only layers. That data belongs to that container and disappears when the container is removed, so it is the wrong place for durable application data.

cards.title: Copy-on-write makes container mutation cheap but not durable
cards.prompt: What happens when a container changes a file from an image layer?
cards.content: The image layer remains immutable. The storage driver presents a writable container layer and records the changed version there. This is efficient for runtime mutation but should not be confused with durable application storage.

cards.title: Named volumes are Docker-managed persistent storage
cards.prompt: When should you choose a Docker volume?
cards.content: Volumes persist independently of a container lifecycle and are managed by Docker. They are a strong default for database files and other application data that should survive container replacement.

cards.title: Bind mounts map a host path into a container
cards.prompt: When is a bind mount appropriate?
cards.content: Bind mounts are useful when host and container must access the same working files, such as source code during development. They couple the container to host paths and can modify host files unless mounted read-only.

cards.title: tmpfs keeps temporary data in memory
cards.prompt: When is tmpfs useful?
cards.content: A tmpfs mount stores temporary data in host memory instead of durable disk. It is appropriate for ephemeral caches or short-lived sensitive material that should disappear when the container stops.

cards.title: Create and mount a named volume
cards.prompt: Persist application data outside the container writable layer.
cards.content: The --mount form is explicit and is preferred for advanced mount options.

code.snippet:
docker volume create app-data
docker run --rm \
  --mount type=volume,src=app-data,dst=/var/lib/app \
  my-api:1.0

cards.title: Bind-mount source code read-only
cards.prompt: How can you expose host source without allowing the container to modify it?
cards.content: Read-only mounts reduce accidental host changes when the container only needs to read files.

code.snippet:
docker run --rm \
  --mount type=bind,src="$PWD",dst=/workspace,readonly \
  alpine:3.22 ls /workspace

cards.title: Choose the storage mechanism
cards.prompt: Which option is usually best for PostgreSQL data that must survive container replacement?

options: The container writable layer
A named volume
A Dockerfile RUN instruction
A temporary environment variable
question.explanation: A named volume persists independently of the database container.

cards.title: Mounts can hide image files at the target path
cards.prompt: Why can files seem to disappear after adding a mount?
cards.content: Mounting a volume or bind mount over a non-empty path obscures the files that were visible there from the image. Recreate the container without that mount or mount at a different target to see the underlying image content again.

cards.title: Back up persistent data intentionally
cards.prompt: What does a real container backup strategy require?
cards.content: Backing up an image does not back up database or volume state. Use application-consistent database dumps or tested filesystem-level procedures, store backups outside the host, and practice restoration.
items: Identify every persistent volume or external datastore.
Use application-consistent backup procedures.
Record schema/application compatibility.
Encrypt and store backups separately from the Docker host.
Define retention and recovery objectives.
Test restoration regularly.

cards.title: UID and GID mismatches cause many mount permission failures
cards.prompt: Why can a container read a path but fail to write it?
cards.content: The process inside the container has a user and group identity that the mounted filesystem evaluates. Align ownership/permissions deliberately instead of falling back to world-writable permissions or running everything as root.

cards.title: Docker bridge networks isolate and connect containers
cards.prompt: What does a user-defined bridge network provide?
cards.content: Containers attached to the same user-defined bridge network can communicate through isolated virtual networking and automatic DNS-based name resolution. Separate unrelated application tiers onto separate networks when useful.

cards.title: Create a user-defined network
cards.prompt: Connect containers on an explicit application network.
cards.content: Using a named network makes connectivity and service discovery easier to reason about than relying on legacy container linking.

code.snippet:
docker network create app-net
docker run -d --name db --network app-net postgres:18-alpine
docker run --rm --network app-net alpine:3.22 ping -c 1 db

cards.title: Container DNS names replace hard-coded container IP addresses
cards.prompt: How should one container address another on a shared Docker network?
cards.content: Use the service/container name or configured network alias. Container IPs may change when containers are recreated, while Docker's embedded DNS resolves current endpoints.

cards.title: Published ports are for crossing the host boundary
cards.prompt: Do two containers on the same Docker network need published host ports to communicate?
cards.content: No. They can connect directly to each other's container ports over the shared network. Publish only the ports that host users or external systems actually need.

cards.title: Host vs container port
cards.prompt: With `-p 8080:80`, which port should another container on the same bridge network normally use to contact that service directly?

options: 8080 on the other container name
80 on the other container name
Always localhost:8080
The Docker daemon API port
question.explanation: Container-to-container traffic on the shared network normally targets the service's container port, not the host-published port.

cards.title: Port publishing can expose services beyond localhost
cards.prompt: Why should port bindings be explicit?
cards.content: Publishing without a host address may listen on host interfaces according to Docker's configuration. For development-only services, binding to 127.0.0.1 can reduce unintended LAN exposure.

cards.title: Inspect network membership
cards.prompt: How do you see which containers and addresses belong to a Docker network?
cards.content: Network inspection is often the fastest way to confirm whether two containers can resolve and reach each other.

code.snippet:
docker network ls
docker network inspect app-net

cards.title: Host networking trades isolation for direct host network use
cards.prompt: When does `--network host` change the model?
cards.content: On supported platforms, host networking lets the container share the host network namespace instead of receiving normal bridge isolation and port mappings. Use it only when the tradeoff is understood and needed.

cards.title: Internal networks can reduce unnecessary egress paths
cards.prompt: Why might a Compose network be marked internal?
cards.content: An internal network is intended to isolate attached services from external connectivity through that network while preserving connectivity among members. It can be useful for private application tiers, subject to platform behavior and other attached networks.

cards.title: Network troubleshooting order
cards.prompt: What should you check before changing application code?
cards.content: Treat container networking as layered: process listening, container port, shared network membership, DNS, and host publishing are separate concerns.
items: Confirm the target process is running and listening on the expected interface/port.
Verify both containers share the intended network.
Resolve the target by service/container name.
Test the target container port, not the host-mapped port.
Inspect published host bindings only for host/external access.
Check host firewall or platform policies when traffic crosses the Docker host.

cards.title: Docker Compose defines a multi-container application
cards.prompt: What does a Compose file describe?
cards.content: A Compose model declares services plus supporting networks, volumes, configs, and secrets. `docker compose` applies that model to create and manage the application's containers and resources.

cards.title: Minimal API and PostgreSQL Compose stack
cards.prompt: How can an API address PostgreSQL by service name?
cards.content: Compose creates a default network and service discovery. The API can use `db` as the database hostname; no database host port is required unless the host itself needs direct database access.

code.snippet:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:devpassword@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:18-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: devpassword
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d app"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

volumes:
  db-data:

cards.title: Compose service names become DNS names on shared networks
cards.prompt: Why should an API use `db:5432` rather than `localhost:5432`?
cards.content: The API and database are different containers. Compose networking resolves the `db` service name to the database container's current address.

cards.title: depends_on ordering is not automatically readiness
cards.prompt: What is the startup-race problem?
cards.content: A process can start before it is ready to accept connections. Use a meaningful health check and a dependency condition such as service_healthy when Compose-level startup ordering must wait for readiness; applications should still handle transient dependency failures.

cards.title: Operate the Compose lifecycle
cards.prompt: Which commands cover the common workflow?
cards.content: Use `up` to reconcile/start, `logs` for output, `exec` for commands in a running service, `run` for one-off service commands, and `down` to stop/remove the project containers and default network.

code.snippet:
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f api
docker compose exec api sh
docker compose down

cards.title: `docker compose down` does not remove named volumes by default
cards.prompt: Why can database data survive `docker compose down`?
cards.content: Named volumes are persistent resources. `docker compose down -v` removes the project's named volumes too, so use that flag only when deleting persistent data is intended.

cards.title: Render the effective Compose configuration
cards.prompt: How can you catch interpolation and merge mistakes before starting services?
cards.content: `docker compose config` parses the project and renders the effective model. Review the output carefully because it may include resolved configuration values; avoid exposing secrets in logs.

code.snippet:
docker compose config
docker compose config --services

cards.title: Compose environment interpolation and container environment are different layers
cards.prompt: Why can `${VAR}` be confusing?
cards.content: Compose can substitute variables while parsing the Compose file, then separately configure environment variables inside services. Know whether a value is used by Compose itself or passed into the container.

cards.title: Compose supports explicit networks for tier separation
cards.prompt: When should you declare networks instead of using only the default network?
cards.content: Explicit networks make topology visible and can prevent services from joining networks they do not need. For example, a public proxy can share a frontend network with an API while the database shares only a backend network with the API.

cards.title: Compose secrets avoid baking secret files into images
cards.prompt: What is the advantage of a Compose secret?
cards.content: Compose can grant a service access to a secret as a mounted file instead of embedding the value into the image. This reduces accidental image/source exposure, though production secret storage still depends on the deployment platform.

cards.title: Compose persistence
cards.prompt: Which command intentionally removes a Compose project's named volumes as well as its containers?

options: docker compose ps
docker compose down -v
docker compose logs
docker compose restart
question.explanation: The -v/--volumes option removes named volumes declared by the Compose application and anonymous attached volumes.

cards.title: Profiles make optional Compose services conditional
cards.prompt: When are Compose profiles useful?
cards.content: Profiles let you include optional services such as debug tools, observability components, or local-only helpers without always starting them in the default application.

cards.title: Compose design review
cards.prompt: Review a Compose stack before treating it as reliable.
cards.content: A good Compose file expresses dependencies and persistence clearly while avoiding unnecessary host exposure.
items: Give each service one clear responsibility.
Publish only ports the host actually needs.
Use service names for container-to-container connections.
Persist databases in named volumes or external storage.
Add useful health checks.
Avoid hard-coding production secrets.
Declare networks when topology matters.
Test `up`, restart, and `down` behavior.

cards.title: Development images and production images have different goals
cards.prompt: Should the production image contain every development tool?
cards.content: Usually no. Development may need compilers, hot-reload tools, test dependencies, shells, and bind mounts. Production should contain the minimum runtime required. Multi-stage targets or separate development configuration can preserve both workflows.

cards.title: Bind-mount source for live development
cards.prompt: How can local source changes appear inside a development container?
cards.content: Mounting the working tree lets the container run host-edited code without rebuilding on every change. Keep dependency and generated directories from being accidentally shadowed.

code.snippet:
services:
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      target: development
    command: npm run dev
    volumes:
      - .:/app
      - node-modules:/app/node_modules
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"

volumes:
  node-modules:

cards.title: Mounting over node_modules can hide image-installed dependencies
cards.prompt: Why does a development bind mount sometimes produce 'module not found' errors?
cards.content: If `/app` contains dependencies in the image and you bind-mount the host project over `/app`, the mount hides the image's `/app` contents. A dedicated dependency volume or host-installed dependencies can avoid the mismatch.

cards.title: Create a reproducible local onboarding flow
cards.prompt: How should a new developer start a containerized project?
cards.content: The repository should document a minimal path from clone to healthy services without manual host database installation.
steps: Install Docker Desktop or Docker Engine plus Compose.
Copy or create the documented local configuration file without committing secrets.
Run `docker compose up --build`.
Wait for health checks to pass.
Run migrations or seed commands through Compose if required.
Open the documented local port.
Use `docker compose down` when finished.

cards.title: Containers make integration tests reproducible
cards.prompt: Why run dependencies in disposable containers during tests?
cards.content: Tests can start known database, cache, or broker versions, run against isolated state, and destroy the environment afterward. This reduces dependence on whatever happens to be installed on the developer machine.

cards.title: Use immutable dependency manifests inside image builds
cards.prompt: Why prefer lockfile-aware install commands such as `npm ci` in reproducible builds?
cards.content: A lockfile-aware clean install follows the committed dependency graph more deterministically than a command that may rewrite dependency metadata. Equivalent deterministic modes exist in other package managers.

cards.title: Development mount tradeoff
cards.prompt: What is the main benefit of bind-mounting source code during local development?

options: It makes the production image immutable.
It lets host edits appear in the container without rebuilding every source change.
It automatically encrypts secrets.
It converts every dependency into a Docker volume.
question.explanation: Bind mounts are useful for rapid edit/run cycles because the container sees the host working tree.

cards.title: Local Docker development hygiene
cards.prompt: Keep the development workflow fast without drifting from production.
cards.content: Development convenience should not leak host-only assumptions or secrets into the production artifact.
items: Pin major runtime and database versions.
Commit Dockerfiles and Compose configuration.
Keep secrets out of images and source control.
Use bind mounts intentionally.
Preserve dependency directories deliberately.
Provide health checks for required services.
Run migrations and tests through documented commands.
Build the production target in CI.

cards.title: Run application processes as a non-root user
cards.prompt: Why add USER to a production Dockerfile?
cards.content: If the application does not need root privileges, running as a dedicated non-root user reduces the impact of a container compromise. Ensure mounted files and listening ports are compatible with that identity.

cards.title: Rootless Docker reduces daemon and container privilege on the host
cards.prompt: What is rootless mode?
cards.content: Rootless mode runs the Docker daemon and containers inside a user namespace without requiring the daemon itself to run as root. It can reduce risk on suitable Linux hosts, with some feature and networking limitations to consider.

cards.title: Never bake secrets into image layers
cards.prompt: Why is `COPY .env` or `RUN echo $TOKEN > file` dangerous during builds?
cards.content: Image layers and build metadata can outlive the container and be distributed through registries or caches. Use build secret mounts for build-time credentials and runtime secret mechanisms for deployed credentials.

cards.title: Minimize the final image attack surface
cards.prompt: How do smaller, purpose-built runtime images improve security?
cards.content: Removing compilers, package managers, shells, test tools, and unused libraries reduces the number of components that can contain vulnerabilities or be abused after compromise. Balance minimalism with operability needs.

cards.title: Drop Linux capabilities you do not need
cards.prompt: What are container capabilities?
cards.content: Linux capabilities split traditional root privileges into smaller units. Docker applies a default capability set, and sensitive workloads can often drop more capabilities rather than relying only on user identity.

cards.title: Harden a simple runtime invocation
cards.prompt: What can a restrictive container run look like?
cards.content: A read-only root filesystem and dropped capabilities reduce writable and privileged surfaces. Add back only required writable tmpfs paths or capabilities after testing.

code.snippet:
docker run --rm \
  --read-only \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m \
  my-api:1.0

cards.title: Pinning by digest improves artifact identity
cards.prompt: Why might production reference an image digest?
cards.content: A digest is immutable content identity, while a tag can be reassigned. Digest pinning improves reproducibility and auditability; an update process must still deliberately refresh pinned versions to receive security fixes.

cards.title: Vulnerability scanning is a gate, not a guarantee
cards.prompt: What does image scanning tell you?
cards.content: Scanners compare discovered packages and artifacts against vulnerability data. Results require triage for reachability, severity, fixes, and false positives; a clean scan does not prove the image or application is secure.

cards.title: Secret handling
cards.prompt: Which approach is safest for a registry credential needed only during an image build?

options: COPY the credential file into the image then delete it later
Put it in a Dockerfile ENV instruction
Use a BuildKit build-secret mount so it is not copied into normal image layers
Commit it to a private Git repository
question.explanation: Build secret mounts provide the credential to the build step without intentionally persisting it in ordinary image layers.

cards.title: Container security baseline
cards.prompt: Apply defense in depth rather than relying on isolation alone.
cards.content: Container boundaries are useful security controls, but exposed sockets, excessive privileges, vulnerable images, writable mounts, and leaked secrets can defeat them.
items: Use trusted and maintained base images.
Rebuild regularly for patched dependencies.
Run as non-root when practical.
Do not bake credentials into images.
Publish only required ports.
Prefer read-only mounts where possible.
Drop unnecessary capabilities.
Avoid mounting the Docker socket into untrusted workloads.
Scan images and dependencies.
Pin or otherwise control production artifact identity.

cards.title: The Docker socket is effectively control-plane access
cards.prompt: Why is mounting `/var/run/docker.sock` into a container high risk?
cards.content: A process that can control the Docker Engine can often create privileged containers, mount host paths, or otherwise gain host-level influence. Treat Docker API/socket access as highly privileged and never grant it casually to untrusted workloads.

cards.title: Build once and promote the same image
cards.prompt: Why should staging and production use the same built artifact?
cards.content: Rebuilding separately for each environment can introduce dependency or base-image drift after tests have passed. Build a versioned image once, test it, then promote that exact digest through environments with runtime configuration supplied externally.

cards.title: Tag and push a release image
cards.prompt: How do you publish a versioned image to a registry?
cards.content: Authenticate using a secure credential flow appropriate to the registry. Prefer immutable versioning conventions and record the resulting digest used by deployments.

code.snippet:
docker tag my-api:1.0 registry.example.com/team/my-api:1.0
docker push registry.example.com/team/my-api:1.0

cards.title: Graceful shutdown protects in-flight work
cards.prompt: What should happen when a deployment stops a container?
cards.content: The application should stop accepting new work, finish or safely abandon in-flight operations, close connections, flush necessary telemetry, and exit before the shutdown deadline.

cards.title: Container health is not full service reliability
cards.prompt: Why are logs and health checks not enough?
cards.content: Production operation also needs metrics, traces or request correlation where appropriate, alerting tied to user outcomes, capacity monitoring, and dependency visibility. Container state is only one layer of service health.

cards.title: Persistent services need backup and recovery outside container lifecycle
cards.prompt: What does replacing a database container prove about durability?
cards.content: Only that the database process can restart. Durable operations require persistent storage, backups, recovery testing, and compatibility across application/schema versions.

cards.title: Resource limits and requests need workload measurements
cards.prompt: How should production limits be chosen?
cards.content: Measure normal and peak CPU, memory, I/O, and latency behavior. Set boundaries that protect the host while leaving enough headroom for healthy spikes, then monitor throttling and OOM events.

cards.title: Immutable containers simplify rollbacks
cards.prompt: Why avoid patching files inside running production containers?
cards.content: Manual in-place changes are hard to reproduce and disappear on replacement. Fix source or configuration, build a new versioned image, deploy it, and retain the prior known-good artifact for rollback.

cards.title: Production image promotion
cards.prompt: Which release practice best preserves what CI actually tested?

options: Rebuild the image separately on every production host
Promote the exact tested image digest
SSH into containers and patch files manually
Use the mutable latest tag without recording the resolved digest
question.explanation: Promoting the exact tested digest avoids rebuild drift between test and production.

cards.title: Production container readiness review
cards.prompt: Before deployment, verify the artifact and runtime contract.
cards.content: Production readiness spans the image, application behavior, persistent state, configuration, and platform controls.
items: Image is versioned and traceable to source/CI.
Base image and dependencies are maintained.
Process runs with least privilege.
Secrets arrive at runtime through an approved mechanism.
Persistent data and backups are defined.
Health and graceful shutdown behavior are tested.
Resource limits are measured.
Logs/metrics are observable.
Rollback uses a known-good immutable artifact.
Deployment records the exact image digest.

cards.title: Docker Compose is useful, but production orchestration is a separate decision
cards.prompt: Does learning Compose automatically mean every production system should run with Compose?
cards.content: No. Compose is excellent for describing and operating multi-container applications in many contexts, but production requirements may call for a managed container platform or orchestrator with scheduling, rollout, autoscaling, secret, and high-availability features.

cards.title: Diagnose a container that exits immediately
cards.prompt: What should you inspect first?
cards.content: Start with evidence from the stopped container before rebuilding or deleting it.
steps: Run `docker ps -a` and note the exit status.
Read `docker logs <container>`.
Inspect `.State` and the configured command with `docker inspect`.
Check required environment variables and mounted files.
Run the image interactively with an alternate command when useful.
Fix the root cause, then recreate the container.

cards.title: Diagnose 'connection refused' between containers
cards.prompt: How do you isolate a networking failure?
cards.content: Connection refused usually means the address resolved and the target host actively rejected the connection because no process was listening on that address/port or it was not ready.
steps: Confirm both services are running.
Verify the target process listens on the expected container port.
Use the target service name, not localhost.
Confirm both services share a network.
Check readiness/health and startup timing.
Inspect application logs for bind-address or startup errors.

cards.title: Diagnose a build cache surprise
cards.prompt: Why did Docker reuse or rebuild an unexpected layer?
cards.content: Build cache keys depend on instructions and relevant input metadata. Trace the first changed or invalidated instruction rather than assuming the cache is random.
steps: Run a normal build and inspect which steps are cached.
Find the earliest step that rebuilt unexpectedly.
Check COPY/ADD inputs and build-context changes.
Check Dockerfile instruction changes.
Use `--no-cache` only when deliberately testing a clean rebuild.
Use `--pull` separately when you need a refreshed base image.

cards.title: Measure container resource use
cards.prompt: Which command shows live CPU, memory, network, and block I/O?
cards.content: Use runtime metrics to confirm whether a container is constrained, leaking memory, or unexpectedly busy.

code.snippet: docker stats

cards.title: Understand image layer history
cards.prompt: How can you inspect the commands and sizes contributing to an image?
cards.content: Image history helps identify unexpectedly large layers, accidental package caches, or files copied too early.

code.snippet: docker image history my-api:1.0

cards.title: Architecture mismatch causes exec-format failures
cards.prompt: Why might an image built on one machine fail on another CPU architecture?
cards.content: An image may contain binaries for a platform such as linux/amd64 while the target is linux/arm64. Use multi-platform images/builds or select the correct platform-specific artifact.

cards.title: A full disk can be Docker state, build cache, logs, or volumes
cards.prompt: What should you inspect before pruning?
cards.content: Use `docker system df` and resource-specific list/inspect commands. Volumes can contain irreplaceable data, so never treat blanket pruning as harmless cleanup.

cards.title: Prune unused resources deliberately
cards.prompt: How can you remove unused Docker objects?
cards.content: Prune commands are destructive. Review what is unused and preserve important volumes and images before broad cleanup.

code.snippet:
docker container prune
docker image prune
docker builder prune
# Review volumes carefully before any volume pruning.

cards.title: Container cannot reach database
cards.prompt: An API container uses `localhost:5432` while PostgreSQL runs in another Compose service named `db`. What is the first configuration fix?

options: Change the database host to `db`
Publish the API on more host ports
Run the API as root
Delete the Docker network
question.explanation: Inside the API container, localhost points back to the API container. Compose service discovery should use the database service name.

cards.title: Do not destroy evidence while debugging
cards.prompt: What should you capture before recreating resources?
cards.content: Containers are replaceable, but their logs and runtime metadata often contain the only immediate evidence of why they failed.
items: Container name/ID and image digest.
Exit code and state.
Recent logs.
Effective environment/configuration excluding secret disclosure.
Mounts and volume names.
Network memberships and port mappings.
Resource/OOM indicators.
Exact command or Compose configuration used.
